title: Using Diffusion Models to Estimate Uncertainties in Analytic Continuation
authors: Sagi Meir, Daniel Freedman, Barak Hirshberg
abstract: Inverse problems are ubiquitous in physics, chemistry, and engineering, arising when reconstructing hidden quantities from indirect measurements. A key example is the analytic continuation of imaginary-time correlation functions (iTCFs) to the real-frequency domain. This process requires an inverse Laplace transform, which is inherently ill-posed and highly sensitive to small input variations. Recent neural network (NN)-based methods have shown promising results by learning mappings from imaginary-time to real-frequency spectra, often outperforming traditional techniques such as maximum entropy. However, because the problem is ill-posed, many spectra fit the same iTCF. Regression-based approaches output a single solution, which approximates an average over the true solution space, and therefore fail to capture the full distribution of plausible power spectra. To address this issue, we introduce a diffusion-based framework for analytic continuation that learns the distribution of spectra consistent with a given iTCF. It offers two key advantages. First, it quantifies uncertainty directly from the learned distribution. Second, by analyzing the spread and structure of this distribution, we can quantitatively assess the intrinsic hardness of each inversion problem. We measure this hardness with a new metric, the uncertainty pseudo-volume. Applying the framework to an iTCF from a path-integral molecular dynamics simulation of liquid parahydrogen, we obtain the self-diffusion coefficient with an error bar and flag a secondary high-frequency peak as a possible spurious artifact. In contrast to previous attempts at uncertainty quantification, our generative approach rests on a concrete probabilistic basis, providing a more theoretically grounded measure of confidence in the reconstructed power spectra.
summary: The paper addresses the challenge of analytically continuing imaginary-time correlation functions (iTCFs) to real frequencies, an inherently ill-posed problem. By employing a diffusion model framework, the authors move beyond simple regression to learn the entire probability distribution of possible spectra consistent with the input iTCF. This allows for rigorous quantification of uncertainty and assessment of the physical ambiguity in the measurement.
main_problem: The core problem is the ill-posed analytic continuation of imaginary-time correlation functions (iTCFs) to estimate real-frequency power spectra.
main_result: The authors introduce a diffusion-based generative framework that models the full probability distribution of plausible spectra, allowing for direct quantification of uncertainty and assessment of inversion hardness via an 'uncertainty pseudo-volume.'
method: They adapt conditional diffusion models (like DiT) to learn $P(C(\omega)|G(	au))$, treating the continuation as a generative sampling task rather than a single regression point estimate.
model_or_system: The methodology is applied to iTCFs derived from path-integral molecular dynamics simulations, exemplified by liquid parahydrogen. The underlying physics involves relating imaginary-time correlation functions $G(	au)$ to the real-frequency power spectrum $C(\omega)$.
key_observables: Self-diffusion coefficient (with error bar), reconstructed power spectra $C(\omega)$, and the uncertainty pseudo-volume.
important_parameters: Imaginary time $	au \in [0,  eta\hbar]$, diffusion time steps ($N=40$), and the conditioning input channels (raw iTCF, log(iTCF), normalized signal, histogram equalization).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the true solution space of compatible spectra can be accurately modeled by a continuous probability distribution learned via diffusion processes.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the non-uniqueness of the inverse Laplace transform using synthetic data. Figure S1 shows Principal Components (PCs) derived from an ensemble, quantifying the variance explained by successive components.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the ill-posed nature of iTCF continuation. It critiques existing NN regression methods for ignoring solution uncertainty. The core contribution is presenting and detailing the diffusion model framework, including its conditional training objective, advanced sampling techniques (DPM-Solver++), and multi-channel input representation.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, theoretically grounded tool for analyzing spectral data in quantum many-body physics by moving beyond single-point estimates to quantify inherent physical uncertainties arising from ill-posed inverse problems.
